Relevant process parts or “nodes” are each matched with a set of common guidewords to identify a likely cause of that scenario as well as a hazardous consequence. These consequences are evaluated individually to determine their severity and likelihood [23, 24]. HAZOP is frequently used as a qualitative risk analysis method and starts with identifying the most relevant process parts (e.g., hydrogen tank, TPRD, etc.) and operation states (e.g., service on fuel system, defueling, etc.). The impact of process unit conditions (e.g., pressure, temperature, etc.) are considered by applying guide words (e.g., more, less, etc.) to determine if a hazard exists for a specific process part and operation state. For all scenarios, the likely consequences and frequency are rated on a relative number scale, and the relative severity of the outcome is often determined by combining the numerical consequence and frequency numbers [24]. HAZOP analyses are commonly used by operational and engineering teams in industry to identify scenarios that can lead to downtime, equipment damage, or safety threats. These analyses frequently reveal opportunities where processes have the potential to deviate from desired conditions due to human error, equipment malfunction, or critical operational changes. Regularly reviewing these hazards may be a requirement for compliance with safety codes and standards or internal protocols [25]. 2.2. Approach The objectives of this work include the identification and classification of relevant safety hazards of hydrogen rail in maintenance facilities, especially considering the performance of pertinent service activities. A qualitative risk analysis HAZOP method was applied to identify the most relevant process parts, operation states, process unit conditions, guide words, consequences, and frequency to determine a resulting quantitative outcome severity for each scenario. Because of their role in containing or delivering pressurized hydrogen, twelve key process parts were considered in the analysis and included the hydrogen tank, associated tank equipment, and fuel cell.
